newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS- JULY 25.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS- JULY 25.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek financial press:

-- National Bank and Alpha Credit Bank, Greece's two largest commercial banks, have turned in spectacular performance in the first half of 1997 on the back of a tough fiscal 1996. Both banks also place emphasis on improving their capital base and capital adequacy ratios.

-- The Bank of Greece announced a cut in its basic and floor depo facility rates by 30 basis points but banking sources said the move would only have a temporary effect. The rates cut is seen taking advantage of the rise in the dollar/mark rate which strengthens the drachma versus the mark and the ecu.

-- Development minister Vasso Papandreou said that tourist arrivals this year will be up between eight and 10 percent. The minister advised Greece's hotel operators to focus on quality and avoid price cuts which will result in lower future revenues.
-- Record profits were announced by National Bank and Alpha Credit with the performance of other expected to follow suit in forthcoming results reports.

-- Negotiations between food manufacturers and retailers with the mediation of the development ministry kicked off with an agreement for a price freeze in an effort to harness inflation. Prices cuts are also on th cards for cereals, dairy products and edible oils.
-- The finance ministry is reportedly contemplating an upward revision of its set of factors for objective determination of taxable income of commercial companies on the basis of their turnover.
-- The key issue of the 1998 budget will be the drastic cut in government debt servicing cost which may ease to as low as 1.5 percent of GDP.

-- Company directors will be rendered personally liable with their private assets for the payment of social security contributions for their employees, alike regulations on tax payments, according to a draft Bill on tax evasion submitted for vote to parliament.

-- Shock waves sent by the dollar's rise in international markets are absorbed and central banks of large countries have refrained from raising their rates. Dealers expect the dollar to appreciate further but the Bank of Greece is not anticipated to step in as its governor has stated that the pre-defined exchange rate policy will be adhered to. --Angelos Kiosklis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
